claims.text: The test material is a single-phase CrFeCoNiAl high-entropy alloy.
The single-phase CrFeCoNiAl alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
The thermodynamic stability of aluminum oxide causes aluminum to oxidize preferentially in CrFeCoNiAl.
Preferential aluminum oxidation produces an external α-Al2O3 scale on single-phase CrFeCoNiAl above 900 °C.
The α-Al2O3 scale is uniform, continuous, coherent, slowly growing, and well bonded to the substrate.
A continuous external layer of a stable oxide can separate an alloy from an oxidizing or corrosive environment.
The α-Al2O3 layer has low oxygen diffusivity and therefore inhibits further oxidation.
The alumina scale has a good lattice match with the underlying CrFeCoNiAl alloy.
The alumina scale minimizes or relieves internal thermal-mismatch stresses.
Low oxygen transport and reduced mismatch stress prevent oxide-scale cracking and spallation above 900 °C.
The single-phase, higher-Al test alloy will exhibit slower oxidation and less cracking or spallation than a lower-Al or multiphase control.
A lower-Al baseline is more likely to form a nonprotective oxide and undergo spallation.
A multiphase CrFeCoNiAl-family microstructure is more susceptible to heterogeneous corrosion or oxidation damage than a single-phase microstructure.
The proposed behavior applies to sustained exposure above 900 °C in controlled oxidizing or corrosive atmospheres.
Dynamic thermal cycling and environmental fluctuations may alter scale persistence relative to controlled laboratory exposure.
The hypothesis is to be tested by comparing a high-Al, single-phase alloy against a reduced-Al or multiphase control under otherwise identical exposure conditions.
Failure of the test alloy to form continuous coherent α-Al2O3 with reduced oxidation and less cracking or spallation than the control would falsify the hypothesis.
